LAN Onboarding Portal (Connection Approval Gate)

LAN Onboarding Portal (Connection Approval Gate)

Status: implemented (checkpoint 41) and verified on real hardware (checkpoint 43). The soft-portal enrollment flow ships in the control panel binary; the onboarding AP + interception harness lives in tools/captive-portal/; gateway-level enforcement is a designed follow-up.

What it is

A captive-style portal hosted entirely inside the control panel (:8082), reachable before a device is approved. A laptop that joins the onboarding Wi-Fi gets:

  1. A welcome page with download links and a live download counter.
  2. joining-cluster.sh (Linux/macOS) or joining-cluster.ps1 (Windows) — the enrollment scripts.
  3. The approval workflow: script registers the laptop → instructor Allow/Deny on the existing admin console (control.ros-platform.local → Instructor console) → laptop switches to the cluster network.

No internet access is required at any point: portal, scripts, and counter APIs are all served from the master laptop.

Network layout

text
onboarding Wi-Fi (AP on master)          cluster router (separate device)
  └─ new laptop, unapproved               └─ approved laptops + K3s traffic only
        │  http://<master-ip>:8082/portal
        ▼
  master laptop
  ├─ onboarding AP (NM AP mode + dnsmasq + nft)  ← tools/captive-portal/
  ├─ K3s (control plane + Traefik)
  └─ control panel :8082 (hostNetwork)
     ├─ /portal                 welcome page (no auth — by design)
     ├─ /portal/joining-cluster.{sh,ps1}
     ├─ /api/downloads/count    public aggregate counter
     └─ /api/downloads/stats    JWT-gated detail for the admin console

Traffic separation is physical: the master hosts the onboarding AP only; the cluster router carries all cluster traffic. The master laptop is never a router.

Enrollment flow

mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant L as New laptop (onboarding Wi-Fi)
    participant P as Control panel :8082 (/portal)
    participant A as Instructor console
    L->>P: GET /portal (welcome + counter)
    L->>P: GET /portal/joining-cluster.sh (or .ps1)
    Note over L: user runs the script manually
    L->>P: POST /api/nodes/register (fingerprint, idempotent)
    L->>P: GET /api/nodes/{id} poll every 5s
    A->>P: POST /api/nodes/{id}/approve | deny
    L->>P: poll returns approved (+ k3s token for Hosts)
    L->>L: switch Wi-Fi (nmcli/netsh or manual)

The scripts (joining-cluster.sh, joining-cluster.ps1)

Both mirror join-cluster.sh's hardware gate (≥8 cores, ≥16 GB, NVIDIA ⇒ Host) and:

  • Find the panel via PANEL_URL env → mDNS (_ldndrc-master._tcp) → interactive prompt.
  • Register with retries. Idempotent: the panel deduplicates by hardware fingerprint, so re-running after a failure reuses the same join request.
  • Poll until approved / denied / expired; denied shows the operator's reason.
  • Attempt the cluster Wi-Fi switch (nmcli --ask / netsh wlan connect) with manual fallback instructions printed on any failure.
  • Approved Hosts are offered the K3s agent install (confirm prompt; sudo; uses K3S_INSTALL_URL, default https://get.k3s.io). Guests stop after approval — browser-only. Windows laptops always enroll as Guests (k3s agents are Linux-only).

The status the script displays comes exclusively from the panel — a client cannot assert its own approval, and actual network access is enforced by the gateway, not by the script or the UI.

--detect-only and test-joining.sh

joining-cluster.sh --detect-only prints the detection/decision lines and exits — no network. test-joining.sh (repo root) runs five threshold scenarios against it, mirroring test-join.sh.

Download counter

Semantics (deliberate)

Metric Counts Visible to
requests Every artifact endpoint hit: HEAD probes, Range/partial fetches, retries, aborted transfers, 304s Admin only
downloads Full 200 GET responses whose entire body reached the client Public (aggregate)
devices Distinct sha256(salt ‖ IP ‖ User-Agent) per artifact Admin only

A served download does not prove anything about the client. The server knows the bytes left the NIC; it cannot know whether the user saved the file, ran it, or whether the transfer was a browser retry. The portal page says this in plain text, and so does this doc. Treat the counter as engagement telemetry, not conversion data.

Storage & accuracy

  • JSON file at DOWNLOADS_DB (default /var/lib/ldndrc/downloads.json), following the nodes.json/sessions.json pattern: mutex-guarded, atomic tmp+rename on every mutation. Concurrent increments are serialized and exact (tested with parallel writers).
  • Persists across server restarts and container restarts. Same caveat as the other panel stores: the Deployment uses an emptyDir volume, so counts reset on pod redeploy. Move all three DBs to a PVC in the same change if this ever matters.
  • A random per-DB salt is persisted with the counts so the unique-device hashes stay stable across restarts.

Privacy

The public count endpoint exposes aggregate totals only. IP addresses, user agents, and device hashes never leave the server; even the admin stats endpoint shows counts, not values. IP+UA hashing is not identity — both are spoofable, and the unique metric is directional. MAC addresses are deliberately not used.

API reference (additions to the panel)

Method Path Auth Purpose
GET /portal, /portal/ none Welcome page (live counter, run instructions)
GET /portal/joining-cluster.sh none Script download (counts served downloads)
GET /portal/joining-cluster.ps1 none Windows script download
GET /api/downloads/count none {"artifacts":{"joining-cluster.sh":N,...},"total":T}
GET /api/downloads/stats JWT Adds per-artifact requests/devices + unique_devices

Also changed: node IDs are now 128-bit (32 hex chars) instead of 32-bit. The ID doubles as the enrollment bearer capability for polls/diagnostics — knowledge of the ID is the token, never IP/MAC. Existing stored IDs keep working.

Onboarding AP setup (master laptop, infrastructure)

Not part of the Go app — the harness that makes the captive prompt real lives in tools/captive-portal/:

bash
./tools/captive-portal/run.sh start   # panel + trap; prints the root steps
./tools/captive-portal/run.sh sudo    # hotspot, dnsmasq, nft (run as root)

What those root steps do:

  1. Hotspot — NetworkManager AP mode on the Wi-Fi interface, pinned to 192.168.4.1/24 with ipv4.method manual. Do not use ipv4.method shared: NM's internal dnsmasq fails to spawn on some hosts (Failed to execute child process "/usr/bin/dnsmasq" (Operation not permitted)) — that was the blocker on the reference laptop.
  2. dnsmasq (run as root, pid file in the runtime dir) — DHCP 192.168.4.50–150 and wildcard DNS address=/#/192.168.4.1, so any http:// attempt resolves to the master.
  3. nftables — iifname <hotspot> tcp dport 80 redirect to :8090, matching the interface rather than a subnet (NetworkManager's subnet can change). The trap answers every intercepted request with 302 → http://192.168.4.1:8082/portal, including the OS connectivity probes (generate_204, connectivity-check.ubuntu.com), which is what triggers the OS "sign in to network" prompt.
bash
# root teardown
sudo nft delete table ip ldndrc-captive
sudo kill "$(cat ~/.local/state/ldndrc-captive/dnsmasq.pid)"
nmcli connection down ldndrc-onboarding

Test panel port: if a deployed control-panel pod already owns :8082 (hostNetwork), start the harness with PANEL_PORT=8083; the trap and printed commands follow that port.

The mDNS advertiser (_ldndrc-master._tcp, already in the panel) also answers "where is the master" for scripts using avahi-browse.

./test-captive-trap.sh checks the redirect contract (302, Location, no-store, body refresh, HEAD/POST) in ~2 s with no root.

Gateway enforcement (designed follow-up)

Approval state lives in the panel; enforcement lives at the gateway. To keep them decoupled (and vendor-neutral), the core deliberately ships no enforcement code. The later integration contract:

text
GET /api/gateway/devices            (JWT or gateway-shared secret)
→ {"devices":[{"id":"…","status":"approved","mac":"…","ip":"…"}]}

A gateway integration (OpenWrt script, hostapd helper, or any router with an API) polls this endpoint and applies allow/deny rules to the radio interface. Nothing in internal/portal or internal/nodes changes; the panel already treats approval as data, not enforcement. Options for extending nodes.Node with mac/last_ip at registration time are described in the checkpoint 41 notes.
